summary:
Trend Detective takes a monthly NASA time series for any region (exported from NASA Giovanni), and answers four questions in plain language:

What is changing, and how fast? Theil-Sen slope per decade with a 95% confidence range.
Is it significant? Mann-Kendall test, plus a version corrected for year-to-year memory.
Could you fool yourself? The Trend Stress Test re-runs the analysis for every window of 15 or more years and every possible start year.
If it is not significant yet, how long until it might be? A simulation of 1,000 possible futures, cross-checked against a published formula.
details:
What it does

Trend Detective is a free web app that takes any monthly NASA climate time series and gives a clear, careful answer to four questions: what is changing, how fast, is it statistically real, and should you believe it?

You pick a NASA variable and a region, then upload or drop in any standard "Time Series, Area-Averaged" CSV file from NASA Giovanni. The app walks through the data across five screens:

  • Investigate: Shows what the variable measures in plain English, its data source, and your chosen region on a map. It calculates the rate of change per decade (with a 95% confidence range) and a Mann-Kendall p-value, then gives a "Detective’s verdict" tagged as significant, borderline, not yet significant, or no clear trend.
  • Stress test: Re-checks the trend across every possible time window of 15 years or more (465 windows in a 44-year record). It reveals the "start-year trap"—showing how the reported trend changes depending on which start year you pick—along with the year a trend became reliable, or how many more years a weak trend needs before becoming significant.
  • Second witness: Tests the same measurement in an independent NASA dataset over the exact same complete years (for example, comparing the AIRS satellite against the MERRA-2 weather model).
  • Compare: Checks whether two datasets—such as two different regions, or daytime versus nighttime temperatures—genuinely move in opposite directions. To pass, both trends must be statistically significant and hold up under testing.
  • How it works: Explains the statistical method, glossary, data limits, and references. Every number on screen also includes a plain-words tooltip when you hover over it.

How it works

  1. Strip out normal seasons: The app subtracts each calendar month's average to calculate yearly anomalies, dropping any year with fewer than 10 months of data.
  2. Measure steady change safely: It calculates the rate of change using the Theil-Sen slope (with a 95% interval) and tests significance with the Mann-Kendall test. Both methods resist extreme outliers and don't assume data follows a bell curve.
  3. Correct for "sticky years": Weather has year-to-year memory—a warm year often carries into the next. Using the Yue & Wang (2004) effective-sample-size adjustment, false alarms across 2,000 simulated trendless series with strong memory drop from 28.5% to 8.0% (aiming near the 5% target).
  4. Estimate years to significance: The app simulates 1,000 possible futures to see how long a weak trend would take to become statistically clear, then cross-checks that number against the Weatherhead et al. (1998) formula. For Delhi (1991–2024), both methods give nearly identical results: 39 and 43 years.
  5. Verify accuracy and speed: On simulated data, the 95% interval captures the true trend 95.2% of the time. Behind the scenes, 42 automated tests verify the statistics against SciPy reference results and check that every screen renders properly. Each analysis runs in under 0.6 seconds.

Benefits

  • Teaches a practical scientist's checklist: Users learn to ask whether a trend survives a different start year, a memory correction, and an independent dataset.
  • Makes "not significant" useful: Instead of hitting a dead end, the app estimates how many more years of data a trend would need to become clear.
  • Makes cherry-picking easy to spot: A single chart reveals how much a conclusion shifts depending on the chosen start year.
  • Accessible anywhere: Works with any NASA Giovanni variable and region, runs free in a browser, and requires no installation or account.

Intended impact

Trend claims should be tested, not just plotted. In a classroom, students can test a news headline ("the city is cooling") against real NASA records in minutes and see firsthand why start dates, year-to-year memory, and a second dataset matter. For the general public, the tool demonstrates how a confident-looking trend can vanish when the start year shifts by a single year—and shows that "not significant yet" is a measurable state, not a dead end.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Language: Python.
  • Libraries: Streamlit (web app), NumPy, pandas, and SciPy (statistics), Plotly (charts), and pydeck (maps).
  • Data access: NASA GES DISC Giovanni.
  • Hosting: GitHub (code) and Streamlit Community Cloud (live app).
  • Development: Built on a standard laptop with no special hardware, using AI-assisted coding openly acknowledged in the README
